newsitem.title: GERMANY: Palm says delayed EMU launch would resolve nothing.
newsitem.headline: Palm says delayed EMU launch would resolve nothing.

text.p: Postponing the 1999 launch date for Europe's currency union would be dangerous as any delay would create new problems rather than solve existing ones, a senior Bundesbank official warned on Tuesday.

Speaking after rumours that Germany might be seeking to abort the monetary union's timetable caused chaos in international markets last week, Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm firmly dismissed talk of altering the schedule.
"Postponing (currency union launch) would not be a solution to existing problems," Palm told Reuters in an interview.
Indeed a delay would be dangerous, particularly for Germany, as such a step could be interpreted to mean European nations would scuttle the entire project -- not just delay it.
"For Germany, postponing the launch would raise anew the dangers of an overvalued mark," Palm added.

After grappling with the negative effects of a very strong mark for many months, German policy-makers have largely welcomed the mark's recent downward correction, praising its impact on Germany's export oriented economy.
Echoing colleagues' comments, Palm said "the strong currency distortions, seen in 1995, have now been fully corrected."
Even as the dollar climbed to 1.71 marks, Palm said Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer's statement that the movement has been an "appropriate correction" was still valid.
Stressing the central bank was not interested in a soft mark, Palm said Tietmeyer's statement would not be invalidated by the mark rising or falling by a few pfennigs.
Palm also brushed off any fears that the weak mark could endanger the Bundesbank's prime goal -- battling inflation.
"Current (mark levels) do not create greater dangers for price stability," Palm said, adding that inflationary pressures were currently not plaguing Germany.
However Palm stopped short of suggesting that the combination of fundamental factors could improve chances for an interest rate cut, which some analysts had predicted.
"There are no factors that would prompt us to veer away from our steady-hand policy," Palm said.
The Bundesbank last cut its money market rate to three percent in August, and eased the discount rate to 2.50 percent and the Lombard rate to 4.50 percent last April.
Turning back to the currency union, Palm welcomed nations' efforts to consolidate finances, saying these would likely make it possible for a larger number to enter the union at its inception.
Already Germany and many European Union nations met three of the four main entry criteria, Palm said, referring to low long-term interest rates, low inflation rates and steady currency rates.
The key to success was for nations to now stick with ambitious consolidation programmes in order to meet the deficit goals, Palm said.
"If Germany sticks by a consequent savings package, there is no danger Germany would miss the entry criteria," Palm said.

Germany would likely be joined by "mark block nations including Austria, Ireland, the Benelux nations (Belgium, the Netherlands and Luxembourg) and France" at the outset of currency union, Palm said, adding he been convinced over the last nine months that the group could be larger.

Steering clear of recent controversy between Germany and Italy over whether the southern nation should be allowed to participate at the start, Palm said it was too soon to make a call on Italy's fate.
European government leaders will determine early next spring which nations meet the entry criteria for monetary union as based largely on nations' 1997 economic data. REUTER
